title: LayerSkip: Enabling Early Exit Inference and Self-Speculative Decoding

data.title: LayerSkip: Enabling Early Exit Inference and Self-Speculative Decoding
data.research_question: How can layer dropout and early exit loss enable early-exit inference and self-speculative decoding to speed up LLM inference?

models_and_data.quote: Continual Pretraining: start with a pretrained model and continue pretraining on 52B tokens from a corpus of diverse data containing natural language text and code.
We experiment using pretrained Llama2 7B (32 layers), with pmax = 0.1, escale = 0.2, Crot,R=8 , and Llama2 13B (40 layers), with pmax = 0.1, escale = 0.1, Crot,R=39 .
We later continually pretrained Llama3 8B on 419B tokens with pmax = 0.1, escale = 0.1, Crot,R=8 , and and Llama3.2 1B on 839B tokens with pmax = 0.1, escale = 0.1, Crot,R=8 .
Pretraining from Scratch: start with randomly initialized model and pretrain on 26B tokens from a corpus of diverse data containing natural language text and code.

We experiment with Llama2 1.5B (a custom small Llama-like model with 24 layers) (see A.1.1 for architecture details) with pmax = 0.1, escale = 0.2, Crot,R=23 and Llama2 7B (32 layers) with pmax = 0.2, escale = 0.2, Crot,R=31 .
Finetuning on Code Data: start with pretrained Llama1 7B model Touvron et al. (2023a) and finetune on 5.2B tokens of CodeLlama Rozière et al. (2023) data mix.
Finetuning on Task-Specific Dataset: start with a pretrained Llama 1.5B (24 layers) and finetune on TOPv2 Chen et al. (2020), a multi-domain task-oriented compositional semantic parsing dataset.
CNN/DM Nallapati et al. (2016), XSUM Narayan et al. (2018) abstractive summarization tasks, and HumanEval Chen et al. (2021) coding task.

key_results.claim: LayerSkip self-speculative decoding achieves speedups up to 2.16× on CNN/DM summarization, 1.82× on coding, and 2.0× on TOPv2.
key_results.quote: show speedups of up to 2.16× on summarization for CNN/DM documents, 1.82× on coding, and 2.0× on TOPv2 semantic parsing task

key_results.claim: Self-speculative decoding obtains speedups between 1.34× and 2.16× depending on model or task.
key_results.quote: We obtain speedups between 1.34× and 2.16× depending on the model or the task.

key_results.claim: On CNN/DM, LayerSkip is faster than Draft & Verify (1.81× vs. 1.5×).
key_results.quote: we are significantly faster on CNN/DM (1.81× vs. 1.5×) and slightly slower on XSUM (1.34× vs. 1.48×).

key_results.claim: Pretraining from scratch reaches 2.16× speedup, exceeding traditional speculative decoding.
key_results.quote: the bigger model has a bigger speedup than the smaller model, reaching 2.16× speedup, which exceeds traditional speculative decoding.

key_results.claim: Code finetuning shows up to 1.82× speedup with no accuracy drop.
key_results.quote: We show speedup of upto 1.82× with no accuracy drop.

key_results.claim: TOPv2 self-speculation reaches 2.0× speedup with high token acceptance rates.
key_results.quote: the model was able to achieve high token acceptance rate, (E = 6: 76.0%, E = 12: 97.2%, E = 18: 98.9%) reaching 2.0× speedup

key_results.claim: KV cache reuse saves 9-20 ms per token depending on task.
key_results.quote: We find that the use of KV cache is able to consistently save us 9-20 ms per token depending on the task.

key_results.claim: Early exit with LayerSkip improves TOPv2 exact match to 77% at layer 12.
key_results.quote: with LayerSkip, early exit inference improves to 77% at layer 12.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Self-speculative decoding requires finetuning or pretraining with the recipe, unlike Zhang et al. (2023).
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: Our self-speculative decoding solution requires finetuning a model or pretraining it with our recipe, while the self-speculative decoding approach propoposed in Zhang et al. (2023) does not require changing a model’s weights.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Hyperparameters pmax, escale, and R require tuning to avoid last-layer accuracy drop.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: The introduced hyperparameters, pmax for layer dropout, escale and R for early exit, requires tuning in order to avoid a drop in last layer accuracy.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Pretraining with layer dropout from scratch requires increasing learning rate, and tuning it can be tricky and time consuming.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: When pretraining with layer dropout from scratch, increasing the learning rate is required to maintain accuracy, and tuning learning rate to get optimal accuracy could be tricky and time consuming.

threats_not_stated_by_authors: The paper evaluates Llama-family models only; it does not test Gemma 4 E2B or models with KV-shared layers 15-34 and per-layer embeddings, so transfer to the lab’s target architecture is unverified.

The self-speculative cache-reuse design assumes draft and verification execute the same early layers in the same order; KV-sharing or per-layer embedding schemes could break or complicate this assumption.
Reported speedups are hardware-dependent (H100/A100, some CPU) and may not translate to the lab’s CPU-only Gemma 4 E2B tracing setup.
The paper does not analyze internal mechanisms such as activation patching, logit lens, induction heads, or factual-recall circuits, limiting direct relevance to mechanistic interpretability.
Early-exit accuracy and last-layer degradation vary across model families and training regimes; the paper reports drops for Llama3 models, so accuracy risks may be larger for other architectures.
The method requires training-recipe changes and hyperparameter tuning; it is not a post-hoc inference-only technique for an already trained Gemma model.
data.relevance_to_lab: Indirect: LayerSkip offers early-exit, layer-dropout, shared-LM-head, and KV-cache-reuse ideas that could inform experiments on Gemma 4 E2B’s KV-shared layers and per-layer embeddings, but it does not study Gemma, activation patching, logit lens, induction heads, factual recall, or CPU tracing.

data.title: LayerSkip: Enabling Early Exit Inference and Self-Speculative Decoding
data.research_question: Can layer dropout plus a shared-LM-head early-exit loss make shallow exits accurate enough to accelerate LLM inference, and can the remaining layers verify and correct those exits through self-speculative decoding?

protocol.step: Use exponential per-layer dropout scaling, with the scaling factor rising from 0.0 in layer 0 to 1.0 in the last layer.
protocol.quote:
We found that the best per-layer
scaling is to increase dropout rate exponentially across layers from 0.0 in layer 0, to 1.0 in last layer, L − 1:

protocol.step: Apply early-exit loss at each layer while using the same LM head for every exit.
protocol.quote: Hence, during training, we augment layer dropout with early exit loss at each layer.

protocol.step: At generation time, execute the first E transformer layers and skip directly to the LM head.
protocol.quote:
When generating each token during autoregressive decoding, we run the first E transformer layers in a model,
and skip to the model’s LM head, i.e., the model’s final output becomes g(xE ).

protocol.step: Self-draft d tokens autoregressively by using early-exit inference.
protocol.quote: In our algorithm, we compute the first d draft tokens through early exit.

protocol.step: Verify the draft tokens using the model layers not used during drafting.
protocol.quote: In our self-speculative decoding algorithm, the self-verification stage critically only requires computing the remaining layers of the model that were not used in the draft stage.

protocol.step: Accept draft tokens through the first disagreement, append the next verified token, and resume drafting.
protocol.quote:
All the draft tokens up till the disagreement point are added to the output along with the next
verified token and the process continues from the draft stage.

protocol.step: Maintain one KV cache across the drafting and verification stages.
protocol.quote:
we are able to effectively maintain a single KV cache for the
draft and verify steps, reducing memory and latency.

protocol.step: Cache the exit-layer query so verification can resume from layer E through the final layer.
protocol.quote:
To further reduce computation of the first E layers, we introduce an exit query cache
that saves the query vector of exit layer E − 1 for verification to directly continue from layer E to last
layer L.

key_results.claim: LayerSkip reports speedups of up to 2.16× for CNN/DM summarization, 1.82× for coding, and 2.0× for TOPv2 semantic parsing.
key_results.quote:
We implement our inference solution and show speedups of up to 2.16× on summarization for CNN/DM documents, 1.82× on coding, and 2.0× on TOPv2 semantic parsing
task.

key_results.claim: In the Figure 2 Llama1 7B example, a token required 23.45 layers on average out of 32.
key_results.quote: For the particular example we present in Figure 2, we find, on average, a token requires 23.45 layers out of the model’s 32 layers.

key_results.claim: Against Draft & Verify, LayerSkip was faster on CNN/DM but slower on XSUM.
key_results.quote:
When comparing with Draft & Verify Zhang et al. (2023) on the common model
and tasks of both approaches, we are significantly faster on CNN/DM (1.81× vs. 1.5×) and slightly slower on
XSUM (1.34× vs. 1.48×).

key_results.claim: The code-finetuned Llama1 7B reached 1.82× speedup on HumanEval without an accuracy drop.
key_results.quote: We show speedup of upto 1.82× with no accuracy drop.

key_results.claim: On TOPv2, self-speculative decoding achieved high token acceptance and a 2.0× speedup at the shallowest reported exit.
key_results.quote:
With self-speculation, the model was able to achieve high token acceptance rate, (E = 6: 76.0%, E = 12: 97.2%,
E = 18: 98.9%) reaching 2.0× speedup.

key_results.claim: For TOPv2 semantic parsing, baseline early exit produced 0 EM, whereas LayerSkip reached 77% at layer 12.
key_results.quote:
model, the model is not able to generate complete and accurate parses resulting in 0 EM. However, with
LayerSkip, early exit inference improves to 77% at layer 12.

key_results.claim: KV-cache reuse consistently reduced per-token time across tasks.
key_results.quote: We find that the use of KV cache is able to consistently save us 9-20 ms per token depending on the task.

key_results.claim: The TOPv2 CPU experiment showed a near 2× speedup.
key_results.quote:
We conduct our task specific fine-tuning on Llama 1.5B to measure decoding
performance on CPU as well, showing a near 2× speed up on CPU as well, presented in Table 11.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: LayerSkip requires finetuning or pretraining with its recipe.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: Our self-speculative decoding solution requires finetuning a model or pretraining it with our recipe

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: The dropout and early-exit hyperparameters require tuning to avoid reducing last-layer accuracy.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: The introduced hyperparameters, pmax for layer dropout, escale and R for early exit, requires tuning in order to avoid a drop in last layer accuracy.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Scratch pretraining with layer dropout requires learning-rate increases, and finding the appropriate learning rate may be difficult and time consuming.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: When pretraining with layer dropout from scratch, increasing the learning rate is required to maintain accuracy, and tuning learning rate to get optimal accuracy could be tricky and time consuming.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Using early-exit loss at every layer during every iteration slows training and reduces final-layer accuracy.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote:
We find that adding early exit loss of all layers at all iterations during training
slows down training and reduces the accuracy of the last layer.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Task-specific TOPv2 finetuning regressed final-layer accuracy by 3%.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote:
We notice a regression in the final layer reducing
accuracy by 3%.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Llama3 continual pretraining showed a larger last-layer accuracy drop than Llama2 despite using more training tokens.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote:
For Llama3 8B and Llama 3.2 1B, we notice a larger drop in last layer accuracy when continually pretraining
with LayerSkip, despite training on more tokens.

threats_not_stated_by_authors: No experiment uses Gemma 4 E2B, so transfer to that architecture, scale, tokenizer, and training regime is unknown.
KV-shared layers 15-34 may violate the contiguous, independently cached prefix assumptions behind LayerSkip's single-KV and exit-query reuse.
The study does not use activation patching, induction-head tracing, or factual-recall tracing to establish causal mechanisms for early exits.
The shared LM-head setup does not directly validate the lab's per-layer-embedding approach, and the two representations may yield different logit-lens signals.
CPU evidence is limited to one small Llama-like model on TOPv2 plus a cache ablation, so broader CPU accuracy and latency generalization is untested.
Most reported speedups were measured on H100 or A100 GPUs and may not transfer to the lab's CPU environment.
The provided results report no confidence intervals, repeated-run variance, or statistical significance tests.
The conclusion says the method led to up to 1.86× speedup, while the abstract and tables report up to 2.16×, creating an internal reporting inconsistency.
data.relevance_to_lab: High methodological relevance: LayerSkip explicitly probes each layer by projecting its output through the LM head, corresponding to the lab's logit-lens operation, and its layer-dropout and shared-head early-exit recipe could test whether Gemma 4 E2B's KV-shared layers 15-34 support useful shallow exits. The KVQ reuse design also raises a directly testable hypothesis for cache behavior in shared layers, while the CPU experiment provides a starting point for CPU-oriented replication. However, all model results are Llama-family rather than Gemma, and the paper provides no activation-patching, induction-head, factual-recall, or Gemma-specific per-layer-embedding validation.
